resident.chief_complaint: Weakness and numbness involving all four extremities and progressive sphincter dysfunction over the last 2 months in a 41-year-old female with no history of trauma.
resident.history: A 41-year-old female with no history of trauma presented with weakness and numbness involving all four extremities and progressive sphincter dysfunction over the last 2 months. Initial cervical noncontrast MRI showed a hyperintense intramedullary cord signal, with differential diagnoses including cervical spondylotic myelopathy and tumor. She was referred for an open biopsy of the cervical spinal cord to document the pathology of the tumor. At the time of transfer, she had severe spastic quadriparesis, markedly greater in the upper than in the lower extremities. Follow-up MRI revealed cervical spondylosis with C5–C6 and C6–C7 cord compression associated with an extensive intramedullary high cord signal and cord enlargement on T2-weighted sagittal images extending from C5 to C7; axial images confirmed the intramedullary signal abnormality. T1-weighted MRI sagittal scan showed the lesion enhanced with contrast at the C5–C6 level.
resident.physical_exam: On examination at the time of transfer, severe spastic quadriparesis was present, markedly greater in the upper than in the lower extremities. Weakness and numbness involving all four extremities and progressive sphincter dysfunction were reported in the history. Detailed motor power, reflexes, sensation, and sphincter examination findings are not documented in the record.

imaging.public_message: I have not seen the films and am reporting only the case record's imaging description: cervical spondylosis with cord compression at C5-6 and C6-7, with extensive intramedullary T2 high signal and cord enlargement from C5 to C7. The record does not state compression direction or stenosis grade. These reported findings correlate highly with the described progressive myelopathic symptoms.

neurology.localization: Cervical spinal cord lesion at C5–C7, likely intramedullary, producing upper motor neuron signs in all four limbs. The upper extremity predominance suggests central cord involvement. Detailed motor, reflex, sensory, and sphincter examination findings are not documented, limiting precise localization.

red_flags.finding: Intramedullary cord enlargement and contrast enhancement at C5–C6 on MRI
red_flags.rationale: This suggests an intrinsic cord lesion (e.g., tumor, demyelination, inflammation) that could independently cause the progressive myelopathy; surgical decompression for spondylotic compression may not address the primary pathology, and biopsy or medical management may be needed.

In compressive cervical myelopathy from C5–C7 spondylosis, lower extremities are typically more affected due to longer corticospinal tracts; upper extremity predominance suggests a central cord or intramedullary process, reinforcing the likelihood of a primary cord lesion rather than compression alone.

neurology.symptom_imaging_mismatch: The imaging shows C5–C6 and C6–C7 cord compression, but the clinical pattern of upper extremity-predominant spastic quadriparesis is atypical for compressive cervical myelopathy at those levels, which would be expected to affect lower limbs more; additionally, cord enlargement and contrast enhancement are not typical for simple spondylotic compression, suggesting an intramedullary lesion that better explains the symptoms.
neurology.public_message: Localization: cervical spinal cord (C5–C7), with upper motor neuron signs in all four limbs. The imaging correlates with myelopathy but also shows an enhancing intramedullary lesion. Match level: medium. Red flags: (1) Enhancing intramedullary lesion (changes_indication) - may be the primary cause, not spondylotic compression. (2) Upper extremity-predominant weakness (changes_indication) - atypical for compression, supports intrinsic cord pathology. No other red flags.

preconditions_for_failure: No improvement or further deterioration in motor or sphincter function after 3 months of intensive conservative therapy.
New or worsening neurological deficits at any point during the conservative trial.
Progression of intramedullary signal abnormality or contrast enhancement on follow-up cervical MRI at 3 months.
Inability to participate in therapy due to pain, functional decline, or medical instability.
physiatrist_opening.public_message: I remain the strongest advocate for conservative care. Given the progressive myelopathy and sphincter dysfunction, surgery is being considered, but before proceeding to irreversible intervention, I propose a formal, time-limited 3-6 month trial of intensive conservative management under close neurological monitoring. This would include supervised physical therapy for gait/balance/strength, occupational therapy for activities of daily living, cervical isometric strengthening, posture education, and avoidance of high-risk activities. The literature on nonoperative management of cervical spondylotic myelopathy reports that a subset of patients—particularly those with mild symptoms and no rapid progression—can stabilize or improve without surgery; however, I acknowledge that severe spastic quadriparesis with sphincter involvement and cord enhancement indicates a poorer prognosis for conservative care. Therefore, I define failure as any of the following: (1) no improvement or further deterioration in motor or sphincter function after 3 months of strict conservative therapy; (2) new or worsening neurological deficits during the trial; (3) progression of intramedullary signal abnormality or enhancement on follow-up MRI at 3 months; or (4) inability to participate in therapy due to pain or functional decline. If any of these occur, I will accept that conservative management has failed and support surgical intervention or biopsy as appropriate. Until then, I hold my stance for a trial of conservative care.

physiatrist_final.public_message: The Deputy Director points to the compressive myelopathy, the enhancing intramedullary lesion, and the progressive sphincter dysfunction as making conservative management high risk. I have already weighed these findings: they are why I set a conservative success rate of only 30% and built strict failure criteria into my proposed trial, including early termination for any new or worsening deficits and mandatory MRI at 3 months. Those safeguards directly address the risk of waiting. I have not seen an argument that waiting under such close monitoring is more dangerous than the risks of urgent surgery itself, nor that the enhancing lesion has a tissue diagnosis that would be lost by a short, structured trial. Therefore I hold my stance for a time-limited conservative trial with defined escape criteria.

vice_opinions.assessment: A 41-year-old woman with a 2-month history of progressive upper-extremity-predominant quadriparesis and sphincter dysfunction. MRI shows cervical spondylotic cord compression at C5–6 and C6–7 with extensive T2 hyperintensity, cord enlargement from C5 to C7, and contrast enhancement at C5–6. The differential diagnosis includes spondylotic myelopathy with myelomalacia/reactive enhancement versus a primary intramedullary lesion (tumor, inflammatory, or demyelinating). Given the rapid progression, severe deficits, and sphincter involvement, a prolonged conservative trial is high risk. I favor urgent surgical intervention to both decompress the cord and obtain tissue diagnosis, but the exact approach requires further imaging characterization.
proposed_options: Urgent posterior cervical laminectomy C5–C7 with instrumented fusion and intraoperative ultrasound-guided biopsy of the enhancing intramedullary lesion, if the lesion is accessible from a posterior approach.

Urgent anterior cervical decompression and fusion C5–C7 (ACDF or corpectomy) with intraoperative ultrasound; biopsy of an intrinsic lesion may require a separate posterior approach, either same setting or staged.

Short-interval additional diagnostic workup (post-contrast axial MRI, full neuraxis MRI, CSF analysis, possibly CT myelogram) followed by surgical decompression and biopsy, without a prolonged conservative trial.
Conservative management trial for 3–6 months as proposed by rehabilitation, with close neurological and radiological monitoring.
vice_opinions.preferred_option: I favor urgent surgical intervention rather than conservative trial. My preferred specific plan is posterior cervical laminectomy with fusion and concurrent intraoperative biopsy of the enhancing lesion, provided the lesion is safely accessible from a posterior approach; if not, I would reconsider anterior decompression.
disagreement_points: There is a genuine dispute about whether the enhancing intramedullary lesion is the primary pathology or secondary to compression-related venous congestion/myelomalacia. The radiologist has not reviewed the films, and the neurologist flags the enhancement as a red flag. We need to resolve this before committing to a decompression-only strategy.

The rehabilitation physician advocates a 3–6 month conservative trial. I believe that is unsafe given severe, rapidly progressive quadriparesis and sphincter dysfunction. I want the director to weigh in on this disagreement explicitly.

We lack critical imaging details—axial cuts, exact location and morphology of enhancement, degree and direction of stenosis, and sagittal alignment—which are necessary to choose between anterior and posterior approaches. We should not let this ambiguity delay surgery, but we must acknowledge it.
deferred_questions_to_director: Do you agree that the risk of waiting 3–6 months is unacceptable and that surgery should proceed urgently?
Should we obtain additional imaging (post-contrast axial MRI, full neuraxis) and possibly CSF studies before surgery, or proceed directly with intraoperative findings and biopsy?
Given the current information, which surgical approach do you favor—posterior laminectomy with biopsy, anterior decompression, or a combined strategy?
vice_opinions.public_message: The imaging shows both compressive myelopathy and an enhancing intramedullary lesion; the progressive severe symptoms and sphincter involvement make conservative management high risk. I recommend urgent surgical decompression with tissue diagnosis. The key unresolved questions are the exact nature of the enhancing lesion and the choice of approach; I have raised these for discussion.

director_rulings.public_message: Colleagues, thank you. Before I rule, I need specific inputs. Dr. Resident, please clarify the exact duration and tempo of symptoms, any prior cervical trauma or surgery, and any history of autoimmune disease or cancer. Dr. Radiologist, please review the actual images and report the axial details of the C5–C7 segment: direction and severity of cord compression, exact location and morphology of the enhancing lesion (peripheral vs central, nodular vs patchy), and any evidence of abnormal cord expansion. Dr. Neurologist, would you proceed to surgery now without further workup given the enhancing lesion, or do you believe a short delay for CSF and detailed imaging is justified? Regarding Dr. Physiatrist's conservative trial: I appreciate the structured failure criteria, but with sphincter dysfunction and rapid progression, a 3–6 month delay is not acceptable; however, I agree that we need more information before an irreversible procedure. Therefore, my ruling is to obtain urgent additional workup: stat post-contrast axial and sagittal cervical MRI with thin cuts, full neuraxis MRI, CSF analysis including oligoclonal bands and cytology, and routine labs including inflammatory markers. We will reconvene within 48 hours with results. If the workup reveals an inflammatory or demyelinating etiology, we will treat medically and avoid surgery; if it confirms compressive myelopathy with secondary enhancement, we will proceed with surgical decompression and biopsy. I am not ordering surgery today.
